h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to identify which settings are strong, weak or neutral, and which parts can be cut off from the outcome by other settings. Build hypotheses mainly from (a) the edited field's current value in the parent, since replacing a strong value with a weak one hurts and filling an empty or harmful slot helps, and (b) conditions that disconnect the edited part, which shrink its effect. When finding flaws, replace any hypothesis whose direction could plausibly reverse because of a competing effect, or whose mechanism relies on partial redundancy between different parts. Ensure varied edit fields and values. State a one-sentence mechanism.

hyps.why: Edge 4 reads from node 1, which is dead when edge 0 is none, so the conv has no signal to process.
Node 1 is disconnected from the input when edge 0 is none, so edge 4 edits are cut off from the outcome.
Edge 1 feeds only node 2, which reaches the output only via edge 5, so with edge 5 removed the conv gain vanishes.
Node 2's output is disconnected from the cell output when edge 5 is none, so the conv gain vanishes.
With edge 0 removed, node 1 gets no input, so edge 2 carries nothing and the edit's effect shrinks.
Reconnecting node 1 to the input revives edges 2 and 4, a far larger gain than upgrading an existing op.
Filling the empty 0-to-2 edge with a strong conv adds a new feature path, unlike replacing an existing op.
Filling an empty direct input-to-output slot with a strong conv gains more than replacing an op that already contributes.
Removing a strong conv edge costs accuracy, while removing a weak op costs little.
Removing a strong conv edge hurts much more than removing a weak or already useless op.
